quiz.question: Why is a familiar SSID not proof that an access point is legitimate?
options: The SSID is always encrypted
An unauthorized access point can imitate a legitimate network name
Every access point must have a unique SSID
A network name proves which organization owns the access point
quiz.explanation: Anyone with a wireless card can broadcast any SSID name. In an evil-twin attack (MITRE ATT&CK T1557.004), an attacker clones the corporate SSID to lure clients into connecting and disclosing credentials.

quiz.question: Which statement about WPA3-Personal is correct?
options: It removes the need for a wireless password in every configuration
It guarantees that every connected device is trustworthy
It uses SAE and improves protections in the password-based authentication exchange
It replaces network segmentation
quiz.explanation: WPA3-Personal replaces the WPA2 4-way PSK handshake with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE - Dragonfly exchange), which prevents offline dictionary cracking of captured handshakes and provides forward secrecy.

quiz.question: What is a key advantage of enterprise Wi-Fi using 802.1X with a suitable EAP method?
options: It can support centrally managed user or device authentication instead of relying only on one shared network password
It removes the need to validate certificates
It makes every connected device an administrator
It prevents all radio interference
quiz.explanation: 802.1X connects to central identity stores (such as RADIUS/Active Directory), allowing individual user or certificate-based device credentials, instant single-account revocation, and role-based VLAN assignment.

quiz.question: Why should guest and IoT devices be segmented from sensitive networks?
options: To let all wireless devices access all internal systems
To limit unnecessary communication and reduce the reach of a compromised device
To avoid updating firmware
To eliminate the need for authentication
quiz.explanation: Segmentation (e.g. via separate VLANs, firewall zones, and client isolation) isolates unmanaged devices, preventing an infected guest laptop or compromised smart-TV from scanning or pivoting into internal servers.

quiz.question: What is the primary role of a Wireless Intrusion Detection System (WIDS)?
options: Replace the wireless authentication protocol
Guarantee detection of all passive radio observers
Monitor wireless activity for suspicious events and possible unauthorized infrastructure
Automatically authorize every unknown AP
quiz.explanation: A WIDS analyzes radio spectrum, beacon frames, and management traffic to detect rogue access points, deauthentication floods, evil-twin impersonation, and configuration violations.

quiz.question: What should a security analyst do when two access points advertise the same SSID?
options: Compare the observation with the approved inventory and investigate supporting evidence
Immediately conclude that the second AP is malicious
Disable every corporate access point
Assume that identical SSIDs are always unauthorized
quiz.explanation: Enterprise WLANs naturally use identical SSIDs across dozens of legitimate APs to support roaming. The analyst must cross-reference BSSIDs, vendor OUIs, security modes, and controller logs to distinguish approved APs from evil twins.

theorySections.title: Wireless Networking Fundamentals and Attack Surface
paragraphs: A Wireless Local Area Network (WLAN) connects devices using radio frequency (RF) transmissions, enabling communication with an Access Point (AP) or wireless infrastructure without physical cabling.
Long range, strong wall penetration. High congestion (only 3 non-overlapping channels: 1, 6, 11). Signals travel far into parking lots, increasing external interception risks.
Shorter range, higher bandwidth. Up to 25 non-overlapping 20 MHz channels. Signal attenuates quickly through physical walls, naturally reducing perimeter leakage.
Massive spectrum (up to 1200 MHz). Requires WPA3 or Enhanced Open by standard specification. Legacy WEP/WPA2 are completely prohibited in 6 GHz.

theorySections.title: Wi-Fi Security Standards: WEP, WPA, WPA2, WPA3, and Enhanced Open
paragraphs: In WPA2-Personal, an attacker within radio range records a client connecting to an AP (or triggers deauthentication), captures the 4-way EAPOL handshake, and cracks the pre-shared key offline at millions of guesses per second using GPUs.

Legacy 802.11 management frames (such as deauthentication and disassociation frames) are unencrypted. Attackers spoof the AP's MAC address and transmit forged deauth frames to kick clients off the network.

PMF (mandatory in WPA3) cryptographically signs unicast and broadcast management frames using a Broadcast Integrity Protocol Key (BIP). Clients drop forged deauthentication frames because the attacker lacks the cryptographic key to produce a valid Message Integrity Code (MIC).

theorySections.title: Wireless Authentication, Credential Management, and Access Policy
paragraphs: Enterprise wireless separates authentication from the physical access point using three distinct roles:
The laptop or smartphone presenting credentials. Must be provisioned with a private client certificate or enterprise user account.
Enforces the port gate. Blocks all IP traffic except EAP authentication packets until the RADIUS server sends an Access-Accept.
Verifies client identities against directory services (LDAP/AD/Okta) and returns dynamic VLAN tags and session encryption keys.
In EAP-TLS, mutual authentication occurs using X.509 digital certificates:

theorySections.title: Wireless Threats: Rogue APs, Evil Twins, and Client Risks
paragraphs: An unauthorized wireless AP plugged directly into an enterprise wired Ethernet switch port (e.g. by an employee wanting wireless access). Creates an unmonitored backdoor bridging past physical firewalls and 802.1X admission controls.

A fraudulent wireless access point set up by an external attacker broadcasting the exact same SSID as a legitimate network. Deceives victims into associating to execute adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) traffic interception and credential harvesting.
Even if the enterprise access point is securely configured, unmanaged client behavior introduces severe risks:

theorySections.title: Wireless Segmentation and Enterprise Wi-Fi Architecture
paragraphs: Authentication controls entry; segmentation controls reach. An authenticated wireless connection must never grant unrestricted network visibility into sensitive internal systems.

In public and guest Wi-Fi networks, client isolation prevents devices associated with the same access point from communicating with each other directly over Layer 2 (ARP, ICMP, broadcast, and unicast traffic). This neutralizes malicious peer attacks such as ARP poisoning, SMB relaying, and local port scanning.

theorySections.title: Wireless Monitoring, WIDS/WIPS, and Incident Response
paragraphs: Passively monitors the RF spectrum across 2.4/5/6 GHz channels. Detects unexpected BSSIDs, rogue DHCP servers, deauthentication bursts, and security mode mismatches without actively altering transmissions.
Actively transmits containment frames or automatically disables switch ports on wired switches where rogue APs are discovered. Must be tightly governed to avoid accidental self-denial of service.
